proposals.title: Reaching 70% Fixed Carbon in Sunflower-Husk Biochar Without Killing the Yield
proposals.markdown:
## Reaching 70% Fixed Carbon in Sunflower-Husk Biochar Without Killing the Yield

**Company:** Suncokret Eko d.o.o., NTP Novi Sad **Faculty:** Faculty of Technology, University of Novi Sad, Department of Applied and Engineering Chemistry **Researcher:** Đorđe Vukelić (Ђорђе Вукелић), Associate Professor **Company contacts:** Dragan Ostojić (process lead), Milica Vranić (head of procurement)

### The problem

Suncokret Eko runs a batch slow-pyrolysis reactor at 500–520 °C and gets a mass yield of roughly 28% with fixed carbon around 55 wt%. German and Dutch buyers need at least 70% fixed carbon for soil-amendment certification. Pushing temperature to 650 °C hits the 70% threshold but drops yield below 20%, requiring about 40% more feedstock per tonne of certified biochar—enough to erase the price premium [C007-CH1]. Extending hold time at lower temperatures has given only modest fixed-carbon gains [C007-CH1]. The company has two years of batch logs (temperature profiles, feedstock moisture, particle size, output quality) and a reactor rated to 700 °C [C007, C007-CH1].

Vukelić's fixed-bed experiments with wheat straw showed that fixed carbon increases from 38 wt% at 300 °C to 72 wt% at 700 °C while yield falls to 24.7%, with BET surface area peaking at 600 °C before declining slightly at 700 °C [SYN-PUB-10347]. A central composite design he ran on corn stover identified conditions where a composite desirability function combining high fixed carbon (≥60 wt%) and high BET surface area was maximised while keeping yield above 28%—showing the yield–quality trade-off is not fixed and depends on the temperature–residence-time combination [SYN-PUB-10356]. He holds a granted patent for a sunflower-husk pyrolysis process that uses staged heating at 8–12 K min⁻¹ to 580–640 °C with an isothermal hold of 55–80 minutes controlled by thermocouple feedback [SYN-PAT-033]. That process addresses almost exactly Suncokret Eko's feedstock and quality target.

### Research questions

1. At what combinations of peak temperature (530–630 °C), heating rate (5–15 K min⁻¹), and isothermal hold time (30–90 min) does sunflower-husk biochar from Suncokret Eko's feedstock simultaneously reach ≥70 wt% fixed carbon and ≥25% mass yield?
2. Does a mild torrefaction pre-treatment (260–290 °C, 30 min) of the incoming husks shift the fixed-carbon–yield response surface enough to relax the peak-temperature requirement while staying above the 25% yield floor?
3. Can a process protocol derived from laboratory results be transferred to the company's batch reactor and reproduce the target quality within ±3 wt% fixed carbon across five consecutive production batches?

### Plan

| Period | Work | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| Jan–Mar 2027 | Vukelić's lab receives representative husk samples from Suncokret Eko's current feedstock contracts; TGA-DSC characterisation to determine decomposition kinetics; review of company's two-year batch logs to identify patterns | Kinetic parameters for current feedstock; annotated log analysis |
| Apr–Jun 2027 | Central composite design experiment (temperature 530–630 °C × hold time 30–90 min, fixed heating rate 10 K min⁻¹) on laboratory fixed-bed reactor; proximate and ultimate analysis of all samples; BET and FTIR on selected points | Response surface models for fixed carbon, volatile matter, and yield |
| Jul–Sep 2027 | Torrefaction pre-treatment trials (260 °C and 290 °C, 30 min) on same feedstock followed by pyrolysis at conditions identified in Q2; comparison against untreated baseline | Assessment of whether pre-treatment shifts optimum to a lower peak temperature |
| Oct–Dec 2027 | Selection of best process window; translation into operating instructions for Suncokret Eko's batch reactor; five validation batches run by Dragan Ostojić using the protocol, with Vukelić's team analysing outputs | Validated protocol; fixed-carbon and yield data from production-scale batches; joint technical report |

### What each side brings

**Suncokret Eko:** feedstock supply (sunflower husks from fourteen contracted farms) [C007]; two years of batch pyrolysis logs [C007-CH1]; batch reactor rated 400–700 °C with temperature logging [C007]; two technically trained staff to run production-scale validation trials [C007]; proximate analysis capability on site [C007].

**Vukelić / Faculty of Technology:** TGA-DSC, fixed-bed reactor, BET, FTIR, and Raman instrumentation [R0992]; prior response-surface work on corn stover pyrolysis [SYN-PUB-10356]; sunflower-husk pyrolysis patent covering the 580–640 °C staged-heating approach [SYN-PAT-033]; decision-support matrix from the Vojvodina biochar project covering over 200 characterised samples [SYN-PRJ-0331]; PYROLINK consortium partners across Italy, Germany, Hungary, and Serbia working on harmonised kinetic datasets and Raman-based certification screening [SYN-PRJ-0332]. Vukelić has limited availability for this project given his current ~0.8 FTE PYROLINK commitments and full teaching load [R0992]; experimental work will be carried out with a graduate student or research assistant under his supervision.

### Why this pair

The company's feedstock is sunflower husks—the exact material covered by Vukelić's patent [SYN-PAT-033]. His wheat-straw data already show that 72 wt% fixed carbon is reachable at 700 °C and that the yield–temperature curve is steep enough to make a well-chosen operating point matter [SYN-PUB-10347]. His corn-stover response-surface study confirms that temperature and residence time interact in ways that a simple one-variable temperature sweep misses [SYN-PUB-10356], which is precisely what Suncokret Eko has been doing without resolution [C007-CH1]. The torrefaction pre-treatment angle is supported by his published two-step torrefaction–pyrolysis work on sunflower husks [SYN-PUB-10354]. Suncokret Eko has a production reactor, feedstock under direct procurement control, and detailed process logs that give the project real industrial grounding from day one [C007, C007-CH1].

### Open questions for the first meeting

1. The patent process specifies pre-drying to below 10 wt% moisture [SYN-PAT-033]; what is the typical moisture range arriving at Suncokret Eko's gate, and is the rotary drum dryer able to hit that target consistently?
2. The company's batch logs cover temperature profiles and feedstock moisture—do they also record heating rate and hold time independently, or is the current reactor controlled only by a fixed end-temperature setpoint?
3. If torrefaction pre-treatment proves beneficial, is there space and budget in the current facility layout to add a torrefaction step, or should that route be treated as a longer-term option?

### Agreed up front (proposal)

**Publications:** Results may be published in peer-reviewed journals. Suncokret Eko reviews drafts 30 days before submission and may request a 6-month delay to allow patent filing; after that period publication proceeds regardless. **IP:** Any process protocol developed that goes beyond the scope of the existing patent [SYN-PAT-033] is jointly owned. Vukelić's pre-existing methods, data, and the patent itself remain his. The company may use the validated protocol commercially without royalty; any licensing to third parties requires written agreement from both sides.

proposals.title: Resolving inconclusive antimicrobial susceptibility results for poultry Enterococcus isolates at Labos Dijagnostika
proposals.markdown:
## Resolving inconclusive antimicrobial susceptibility results for poultry Enterococcus isolates at Labos Dijagnostika

**Company:** Labos Dijagnostika a.d., Subotica [C085] 
**Faculty:** Faculty of Agriculture, University of Novi Sad, Department of Veterinary Medicine 
**Company contact:** Dragana Molnar, senior microbiologist [C085] 
**Academic lead:** Nikola Bulatović (Никола Булатовић), Associate Professor [R0056] 
**Suggested duration:** 12 months, January–December 2027

---

### The problem

Labos Dijagnostika's veterinary microbiology line has grown 40% in revenue over two years, driven mainly by poultry farms in the Subotica and Senta areas [C085-CH2]. Enterococcus strains from those farms repeatedly return inconclusive or borderline susceptibility results on the company's card-based automated system. The company suspects this is because the breakpoints currently applied come from human clinical guidelines rather than veterinary-specific references, but no one on staff has practical experience with EUCAST veterinary breakpoint tables or epidemiological cut-off values (ECOFFs) for livestock isolates [C085-CH2]. Labos Dijagnostika holds archived poultry Enterococcus isolates going back 18 months that have not been systematically re-tested [C085-CH2].

Bulatović's group applies EUCAST clinical breakpoints and ECOFFs to field isolates of Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium from swine, poultry, and cattle in Vojvodina [R0056]. A 2022 book chapter co-authored by Bulatović addresses exactly the interpretive gap Labos Dijagnostika faces: the limited availability of veterinary-specific breakpoints and the methodological pitfalls of applying clinical criteria to food-animal isolates [SYN-PUB-00746]. His 2015 study demonstrated BMD as the reference method for resolving disk diffusion errors for a specific drug–pathogen combination (nitrofurantoin/Enterococcus), where disk diffusion produced very-major error rates above 10% [SYN-PUB-00740].

---

### Research questions

1. For which antimicrobial agents does the card-based system at Labos Dijagnostika produce categorical disagreement of more than 10% relative to BMD reference results, when tested on the archived poultry Enterococcus isolates?
2. Which EUCAST ECOFFs or veterinary-specific breakpoints, substituted for the current human clinical breakpoints, reduce the proportion of inconclusive calls to below 5% for those agents?
3. Do the archived isolates carry resistance genes (e.g. tet(M), erm(B), vancomycin-resistance determinants) that predict phenotypic MIC distributions deviating from the patterns observed in the VETO-AMR genomic dataset for Vojvodina livestock Enterococcus [SYN-PRJ-0251]?

---

### Plan

| Period | Activity | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| Jan–Mar 2027 | Labos Dijagnostika ships the archived poultry isolates (up to 18 months of stock) to Bulatović's lab; joint selection of a representative panel of ≥150 isolates by species (E. faecalis / E. faecium) and farm origin; agree the BMD panel (antimicrobial agents and concentration ranges) | Signed material transfer agreement; finalised BMD panel list |
| Apr–Jun 2027 | BMD testing of the full isolate panel in Bulatović's lab using cation-adjusted Mueller–Hinton broth with lysed horse blood, EUCAST quality control strains, and the agreed concentration ranges; PCR or targeted sequencing for key resistance genes | BMD MIC dataset; resistance gene screening results |
| Jul–Sep 2027 | Categorical comparison of BMD results against original card-based results from Labos Dijagnostika's LIMS; identification of agents with very-major or major error rates above 10%; draft revised interpretive criteria using EUCAST ECOFFs | Comparative error-rate table; draft breakpoint recommendations |
| Oct–Dec 2027 | Labos Dijagnostika tests a 30-isolate validation set using the revised interpretive criteria on its card system, with Molnar and Bulatović reviewing results; Bulatović drafts a standard operating procedure (SOP) for Enterococcus AST interpretation in the veterinary section; final report prepared | Validated SOP; final project report; draft manuscript for submission |

---

### What each side brings

**Labos Dijagnostika** provides the archived poultry Enterococcus isolates and their original card-based susceptibility records, access to the Deltasoft LabCenter LIMS for export of historical results [C085], staff time from Dragana Molnar and up to two laboratory specialists for the validation phase [C085], and knowledge of the operational constraints of a high-throughput diagnostic setting.

**Bulatović's group** provides BMD reference testing capacity, EUCAST quality control protocols, and access to genomic and resistance gene data from the VETO-AMR project covering swine, cattle, and poultry isolates from Vojvodina [SYN-PRJ-0251], as well as the joint resistance database generated through the ENTRODAN cross-border surveillance work [SYN-PRJ-0250]. Bulatović led the work package responsible for harmonising broth microdilution panels and EUCAST ECOFF application across partner laboratories [SYN-PRJ-0250] and has co-authored work on the methodological challenges of applying clinical breakpoints to food-animal Enterococcus [SYN-PUB-00746].

---

### Why this pair

The specific gap at Labos Dijagnostika — card-system results interpreted against human clinical breakpoints for poultry enterococci — maps directly onto Bulatović's documented expertise. He has applied EUCAST ECOFFs to E. faecalis and E. faecium from livestock in Vojvodina [R0056], co-authored a methodological reference on breakpoint interpretation for food-animal isolates [SYN-PUB-00746], demonstrated BMD as the reference method for resolving disk diffusion errors for a specific drug–pathogen combination (nitrofurantoin/Enterococcus) where very-major error rates exceeded 10% [SYN-PUB-00740], and led the work package responsible for harmonising broth microdilution panels and EUCAST application across partner laboratories [SYN-PRJ-0250]. The VETO-AMR project, which runs through 2025, includes poultry farms and generates whole-genome sequencing data on livestock Enterococcus that will provide a genomic comparison baseline for interpreting resistance gene findings [SYN-PRJ-0251]. Both parties are based in Vojvodina, which simplifies isolate transfer and site visits. Bulatović has stated a preference for clearly scoped collaborations with defined deliverables, which matches the structured nature of this project [R0056].

---

### Open questions for the first meeting

1. How many of the archived isolates have species-level identification (E. faecalis vs. E. faecium) already confirmed, and what antimicrobial agents were included in the original card panel? This determines whether re-identification is needed before BMD testing.
2. Which antimicrobial agents matter most to the poultry farm clients — for example, is ampicillin, tetracycline, or a specific aminoglycoside causing the most operational problems — so the BMD panel can be prioritised accordingly?
3. Does Labos Dijagnostika's ISO 15189 scope currently cover BMD as a method, or would adding it require an accreditation extension that could affect how the validated SOP is deployed?

---

### Agreed up front (proposed)

**Publications:** Both parties are listed as co-authors on any manuscript arising from the project. Labos Dijagnostika reviews the manuscript before submission and may request a 60-day delay if commercially sensitive data are involved.

**IP:** The revised interpretive criteria and SOP are jointly owned. Labos Dijagnostika may implement them in its diagnostic operations without restriction. Bulatović's group may use the anonymised MIC dataset for academic publication and for comparison with the VETO-AMR genomic dataset [SYN-PRJ-0251], with Labos Dijagnostika's agreement on the anonymisation approach.
openIssues: "His 2015 study demonstrated BMD as the reference method for resolving disk diffusion errors for a specific drug–pathogen combination (nitrofurantoin/Enterococcus), where disk diffusion produced very-major error rates above 10%": The 2015 study (SYN-PUB-00740) was conducted on cattle isolates, not a generic Enterococcus study. The draft omits this specificity, implying broader applicability than the source states. Fix: Specify that the study used cattle Enterococcus isolates: 'his 2015 study on cattle Enterococcus isolates demonstrated BMD as the reference method…'

"Bulatović led the work package responsible for harmonising broth microdilution panels and EUCAST ECOFF application across partner laboratories [SYN-PRJ-0250]": SYN-PRJ-0250 says Bulatović led the work package for 'microbiological methods harmonisation', not specifically 'harmonising broth microdilution panels and EUCAST ECOFF application'. The draft adds specificity not stated in the source. Fix: Use the source's language: 'led the work package responsible for microbiological methods harmonisation, ensuring identical broth microdilution panels and consistent EUCAST ECOFF application'.

proposals.title: ML-DSA and Hybrid Signature Integration for the KL-HSM Firmware on ARM Cortex-M7
proposals.markdown:
## ML-DSA and Hybrid Signature Integration for the KL-HSM Firmware on ARM Cortex-M7

**Company:** Kriptolog a.d., Novi Sad [C086] 
**Faculty:** Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, Department of Computing and Control Engineering 
**Academic supervisor:** Milica Nikolić (Милица Николић), Full Professor [R0503] 
**Industrial supervisor:** the company's lead cryptographic firmware engineer, to be named 
**PhD candidate:** to be recruited from Kriptolog's engineering team or as a new hire through the NTP Novi Sad industrial PhD scheme

---

### The problem

Kriptolog's KL-HSM product line — specifically the KL-300 and KL-500 series — uses RSA and ECDSA for all firmware signing operations [C086]. The firmware runs on an ARM Cortex-M7 microcontroller with constrained flash and RAM [C086-P2]. Two national-level agencies and a payment network operator have formally asked, in writing, whether these signing operations will remain secure against quantum-capable adversaries [C086-CH1]. Kriptolog has had one engineer studying the NIST post-quantum standardisation documents and doing prototype work with ML-DSA, but the firmware architecture has not been changed to handle the larger key material and different signature flows that ML-DSA requires [C086-CH1]. A straight drop-in replacement is not possible on the current microcontroller [C086-CH1]. Without a tested, documented migration path, Kriptolog cannot give a credible answer to clients who are planning five- to ten-year infrastructure cycles [C086-CH1], and its planned post-quantum-ready firmware branch remains blocked [C086].

Nikolić's research group focuses precisely on implementing and benchmarking post-quantum cryptographic primitives — particularly lattice-based schemes — on microcontrollers and dedicated hardware security modules with tight memory and power budgets [R0503]. She served as principal investigator on a Science Fund project investigating performance and security constraints of deploying post-quantum algorithms on hardware security modules in Serbian critical infrastructure [SYN-PRJ-0502], and she leads Work Package 3 of SECURED-ICS, a Horizon Europe project covering hardware-level implementation and benchmarking of NIST-standardised post-quantum schemes on programmable logic controllers and remote terminal units [SYN-PRJ-0503]. She has co-authored work on a hybrid classical/post-quantum HSM architecture using an Infineon SLE97 secure microcontroller paired with an FPGA for Kyber-768 key encapsulation [SYN-PUB-05920], and has surveyed implementation strategies for post-quantum algorithms on devices with under 64 kB RAM and under 256 kB flash [SYN-PUB-05918].

---

### Research questions

1. What memory layout and arithmetic optimisations allow ML-DSA (FIPS 204) signing and verification to run within the KL-500's Cortex-M7 flash and RAM budget while meeting Kriptolog's latency targets for PKCS#11 sign operations — and how do those figures compare to the same operations measured with the PQBench-Embed methodology across its four targets (Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M4, RISC-V RV32IMC, and ESP32) [SYN-PUB-05923]?

2. What hybrid signature scheme — combining ECDSA with ML-DSA in a single PKCS#11 transaction — minimises the backward-compatibility disruption for existing clients while satisfying the security claims needed for Common Criteria EAL4+ documentation [C086], and can the design be validated against the test-vector and timing datasets produced in SYN-PRJ-0503?

3. Which side-channel countermeasures (masking, shuffling, constant-time modular reduction) are necessary and sufficient for ML-DSA on the KL-500 hardware at the threat level assumed in a Common Criteria EAL4+ evaluation, and what is the measurable cost of each countermeasure in cycles and stack bytes?

---

### Plan

| Period | Activity | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 2027 | Candidate studies KL-500 firmware architecture; Nikolić's lab and Kriptolog jointly define memory budget, latency targets, and PKCS#11 interface constraints; select two or three candidate ML-DSA parameter sets for evaluation | Written requirements document signed off by both supervisors |
| Q2 2027 | Port reference ML-DSA implementation (drawing on the open-source libraries from SYN-PRJ-0502) to Cortex-M7 bare-metal; profile stack usage, flash footprint, and signing latency using PQBench-Embed harness [SYN-PUB-05923]; identify bottlenecks | Benchmark report with raw numbers for each parameter set |
| Q3 2027 | Apply memory optimisations (in-place NTT, reduced-width polynomial arithmetic, stack-reuse across subroutines); re-benchmark; compare against Q2 baseline | Optimised C implementation committed to project repository; updated benchmark table |
| Q4 2027 | Design hybrid ECDSA + ML-DSA signature flow within PKCS#11 command set; implement prototype; test against Kriptolog's existing client-side software | Prototype hybrid signing firmware running on KL-500 evaluation board; test report |
| Q1–Q2 2028 | Side-channel analysis: power trace collection on KL-500 hardware; assess leakage in polynomial arithmetic; implement and measure cost of countermeasures identified in research question 3 | Side-channel evaluation report; hardened implementation |
| Q3 2028 | Fault-injection testing of the hybrid scheme; harden where needed; produce cryptographic design rationale document in the format required for Common Criteria evidence | CC-ready design rationale document; fault-injection test report |
| Q4 2028 | Client-facing migration guide: key sizes, certificate profile changes, hybrid operation period, rollback procedure; internal firmware integration into KL-500 release branch | Draft migration guide reviewed by Kriptolog's two agency clients; firmware branch merged |
| Q1–Q2 2029 | Performance and correctness regression testing using the toolchain-aware harness approach from EMBIVAL [SYN-PRJ-0353]; write up PhD thesis chapters 1–3 | Regression test suite; draft chapters |
| Q3–Q4 2029 | Submit two journal papers (target: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security; ACM Transactions on Embedded Computing Systems); complete thesis; internal review | Submitted manuscripts; full thesis draft |
| Q1–Q2 2030 | Thesis corrections and defence; final handover of firmware and documentation to Kriptolog | Defended PhD thesis; production-ready post-quantum firmware branch |

---

### What each side brings

**Kriptolog a.d.** provides: the KL-500 evaluation hardware and its firmware source code; access to the PKCS#11 test suite and client-side software used in production; the engineer who has already done prototype ML-DSA work [C086-CH1], who is the natural candidate or first collaborator; Common Criteria evaluation methodology expertise [C086]; and the company's relationship with two national agencies and a payment network operator, which creates a realistic validation context for the migration guide.

**Milica Nikolić and her lab** provide: the open-source libraries and benchmarking dataset from SYN-PRJ-0502 [SYN-PRJ-0502]; the PQBench-Embed suite and its baseline data covering Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M4, RISC-V RV32IMC, and ESP32, which will serve as cross-architecture reference points [SYN-PUB-05923]; the hybrid HSM architecture design experience from SYN-PUB-05920 [SYN-PUB-05920]; side-channel and fault-injection evaluation infrastructure developed over the SECURED-ICS project [SYN-PRJ-0503]; and supervision capacity for a fifth industrial PhD from late 2025 onward [R0503].

Kriptolog should supply at least two KL-500 evaluation boards to the university lab. Nikolić's lab has limited availability of Infineon SLE97 kits (two units) [R0503]; the Cortex-M7 boards from Kriptolog would fill that gap directly.

---

### Why this pair

Nikolić's group has been working the exact problem Kriptolog faces — post-quantum algorithms on memory-constrained HSM hardware — from the academic side for several years. She led a national project on deploying post-quantum algorithms on HSMs used in critical infrastructure [SYN-PRJ-0502] and currently leads the hardware implementation work package in a Horizon Europe project targeting the same hardware class [SYN-PRJ-0503]. The hybrid HSM architecture she co-authored combines a secure microcontroller (Infineon SLE97) with FPGA acceleration for post-quantum operations and achieved 38 ms end-to-end hybrid key exchange for a Kyber-768 KEM scheme [SYN-PUB-05920] — an analogous, though not identical, engineering problem to the signing integration Kriptolog needs. Her survey of PQC on constrained devices [SYN-PUB-05918] covers the sub-64 kB RAM, sub-256 kB flash regime that maps onto the KL-HSM constraints. Kriptolog brings the production hardware, the client validation context, and the Common Criteria documentation requirement that will make the PhD output immediately usable rather than a proof of concept.

---

### Open questions for the first meeting

1. What are the exact flash and RAM figures available for the cryptographic stack on the KL-500 Cortex-M7, and what is the maximum acceptable latency for a PKCS#11 C_Sign call in the clients' integration environments?

2. Do the two agency clients and the payment network operator have a deadline — contractual or regulatory — by which a post-quantum migration plan must be submitted, and does that deadline constrain the PhD timeline or require an interim technical report before the full work is complete?

3. PQBench-Embed covers four targets — Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M4, RISC-V RV32IMC, and ESP32 [SYN-PUB-05923]; how much of that data can be reused as baselines for the Cortex-M7, and will Kriptolog make the KL-500 board available to the lab within the first quarter so joint benchmarking can begin in Q2 2027?

---

### Agreed up front (publication and IP, as a proposal)

**IP:** Optimised firmware code written by the candidate and integrated into the KL-500 release branch is Kriptolog's proprietary work product. Algorithmic methods, benchmarking data, and side-channel evaluation results that do not disclose firmware implementation details or product-specific constants may be published freely.

**Publication:** The candidate and Nikolić may publish journal and conference papers based on the benchmarking, optimisation, and side-channel work. Kriptolog reviews manuscripts within 30 days and may request redaction of specific implementation details that would compromise Common Criteria evaluation confidentiality or client security. Neither party may unreasonably withhold consent to publish after redaction.

**Thesis:** The PhD thesis may describe all technical work. Kriptolog may designate specific appendices (e.g., firmware memory maps, client interface specifications) as confidential, to be held by the university under standard restricted-access rules for a period of three years after defence.
openIssues: "the open-source libraries and benchmarking dataset from SYN-PRJ-0502": SYN-PRJ-0502 outputs include an open benchmarking dataset and two software libraries, but the source does not describe them as having been used for ML-DSA or as directly portable to Cortex-M7. The claim that these are what the lab 'provides' to this project is a plan, not a fact — acceptable. However the draft also says 'drawing on the open-source libraries from SYN-PRJ-0502' in the plan table as if those libraries contain ML-DSA implementations; the source only says two software libraries were released, not that they cover ML-DSA. Fix: Do not specify that the SYN-PRJ-0502 libraries contain ML-DSA implementations; just refer to them as the project's open-source cryptographic libraries.

"side-channel and fault-injection evaluation infrastructure developed over the SECURED-ICS project": SYN-PRJ-0503 does not mention side-channel or fault-injection evaluation infrastructure. Side-channel and fault-injection work is mentioned in SYN-PRJ-0502, not SYN-PRJ-0503. Fix: Attribute side-channel and fault-injection infrastructure to SYN-PRJ-0502, not SYN-PRJ-0503.

proposals.title: Widening the mLLDPE Seal Window from 8°C to at Least 20°C for High-Speed VFFS Lines
proposals.markdown:
## Widening the mLLDPE Seal Window from 8°C to at Least 20°C for High-Speed VFFS Lines

**Company:** FlexiPack Solutions d.o.o., Novi Sad **Faculty:** Faculty of Technology, University of Novi Sad, Department of Chemical Engineering **Researcher:** Bojan Grbić (Бојан Грбић), Senior Research Associate **Company contact:** Jovana Mirković, founder and technical director

### The problem

FlexiPack's current seal layer is an mLLDPE sourced from an Austrian supplier [C058]. Acceptable seal strength (measured in N/15 mm) is achieved only between 130 and 138°C — a window of 8°C [C058-CH3]. Below 130°C the bond is unreliable; above 138°C the film deforms and cannot be peeled by the end user. Customers running VFFS lines faster than FlexiPack's film can handle need shorter jaw dwell times, which in practice means higher jaw temperatures, pushing the process outside the current window [C058-CH3]. FlexiPack has tested two mLLDPE types and one blend with LDPE with no significant improvement, and holds DSC curves and seal-strength data (N/15 mm vs. temperature and dwell time) for all three formulations [C058-CH3].

### Research questions

1. Which blend addition — VLDPE at 10–25 wt%, EVA at 10–20 wt%, or a combination — reduces seal-initiation temperature (SIT) by at least 5°C relative to FlexiPack's current mLLDPE while keeping plateau seal strength above 25 N/25 mm, as measured on a laboratory gradient heat-sealer at 0.4 s dwell and 0.3 N/mm² jaw pressure?
2. Does increasing the seal-layer thickness from the current gauge to 20 µm in a coextruded structure provide an additive reduction in SIT on top of the blend modification, as determined by comparing films extruded on both the Faculty cast-film line and FlexiPack's pilot extrusion line?
3. Can a response-surface model (central composite design, ≥15 runs) over the blend-ratio space predict a formulation that delivers a usable sealing window of ≥20°C (target: 125–145°C) with peel force remaining below 15 N/25 mm at 145°C?

### Plan

| Period | Activity | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Jan–Mar 2027 | Grbić's group characterises FlexiPack's three existing formulations by DSC and capillary rheometry; FlexiPack transfers all existing seal-strength and DSC data [C058-CH3] | Baseline rheological and thermal profiles for all three starting materials; identified gap vs. target window |
| Apr–Jun 2027 | Faculty cast-film line produces binary blends (mLLDPE + VLDPE at 10, 15, 20 wt%; mLLDPE + EVA at 10, 15, 20 wt%) at fixed 40 µm gauge; gradient heat-sealer measures SIT and plateau seal strength for each | Screening data set; two or three candidate blend directions selected |
| Jul–Sep 2027 | Central composite design (RSM) over selected blend-ratio space; 15–20 cast-film runs on Faculty line; heat-seal and hot-tack testing; peel-mode analysis at upper temperature limit | RSM model with R² target ≥0.90 for SIT and plateau seal strength; identification of optimal blend region |
| Oct–Dec 2027 | FlexiPack extrudes optimal blend on its pilot extrusion line [C058] at two seal-layer thicknesses; seal-strength and peel testing under conditions matching customer VFFS dwell times; Grbić's group provides rheological support | Validation data set confirming whether ≥20°C window and peel-ability targets are met at production-representative conditions |

### What each side brings

**FlexiPack** provides: the current mLLDPE granulate and supplier datasheets [C058]; DSC curves and seal-strength data for three tested formulations [C058-CH3]; pilot extrusion and lamination line for production-representative film trials [C058]; Jovana Mirković's direct knowledge of the VFFS customer requirements.

**Grbić's group** provides: laboratory cast-film line (45 mm screw), gradient heat-sealer, Brabender plastograph, and capillary rheometer [R0715]; RSM experimental design and statistical modelling expertise demonstrated in ternary mLLDPE/EVA/LDPE work [SYN-PUB-08002]; prior data showing that VLDPE at 20 wt% lowered SIT by 9°C and enabled 26 N/25 mm plateau seal strength at 108°C in mLLDPE films [SYN-PUB-08004]; hot-tack window data from OPP/tie/mLLDPE structures across seal-layer thicknesses [SYN-PUB-07999]; a granted patent covering blend compositions that achieve SIT below 100°C in cast polyolefin films [SYN-PAT-054].

### Why this pair

Grbić's group has worked directly on the two mechanisms most relevant to FlexiPack's problem. In a documented formulation development exercise, VLDPE at 20 wt% lowered SIT by 9°C and enabled 26 N/25 mm plateau seal strength at 108°C in a commercial mLLDPE monolayer film [SYN-PUB-08004]. RSM over ternary polyolefin blends produced regression models with R² above 0.91 for SIT, plateau seal strength, and hot-tack [SYN-PUB-08002]. Seal-layer thickness as an independent variable has also been quantified: a 20 µm seal layer in a three-layer laminate produced a 28°C hot-tack window, compared with 16°C at 10 µm [SYN-PUB-07999]. FlexiPack's existing DSC data and granulate samples give the project a defined starting point rather than a blank-slate materials search. Grbić has noted a preference for collaborations that can access production-scale extrusion equipment [R0715], and FlexiPack's pilot extrusion and lamination line addresses that directly [C058].

### Open questions for the first meeting

1. FlexiPack's seal-strength data are in N/15 mm; Grbić's published work uses N/25 mm. Which strip width will be the project standard, and does FlexiPack's heat-seal tester support both?
2. The Austrian mLLDPE supplier may have technical data on comonomer type and distribution — can FlexiPack share the full resin datasheet, and is the supplier open to discussing alternative grades directly?
3. FlexiPack's customers require easy-peel performance; is there a defined upper peel-force limit (in N/15 mm or N/25 mm) already in a customer specification, or does this need to be established during the project?

### Agreed up front (proposal)

**Publications:** Results may be published in peer-reviewed journals after a 90-day review period during which FlexiPack can request redaction of specific formulation details it considers commercially sensitive. Authorship follows contribution; Jovana Mirković or a named FlexiPack technologist is included if they contribute to experimental design or data collection.

**IP:** Any new blend formulation developed and validated specifically on FlexiPack's materials during this project belongs to FlexiPack. Background IP (including [SYN-PAT-054] and prior published methods) remains with the Faculty. If the project produces a patentable result that builds directly on the Faculty's background IP, a co-ownership arrangement with a negotiated licence fee for commercial use by FlexiPack is the proposed default.
